title: The Caesar salad was born in Tijuana
hook: A salad named after an Italian chef, invented in Mexico, for Americans.
peek: The Caesar salad is not named after Julius Caesar. It comes from Caesar Cardini, an Italian immigrant who ran a restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico, where Americans crossed the border during Prohibition.
lede: The Caesar salad has nothing to do with Rome. Its name comes from Caesar Cardini, an Italian immigrant who ran restaurants in San Diego and in Tijuana, Mexico. During Prohibition, Americans crossed the border to eat and drink freely, and Cardini's restaurant was popular. The salad seems to have been born there in the 1920s, tossed at the table in front of the diners.

bullets.text: Cardini's daughter Rosa said he invented it on a busy July 4th in 1924, improvising with what was left in the kitchen. It is family lore, and his brother Alex claimed a role too.

Accounts describe whole romaine leaves meant to be eaten by hand, dressed with olive oil, lemon, coddled egg, Parmesan, garlic, croutons and Worcestershire sauce. Anchovies, now a standard part of most versions, are usually said to have been absent.
Even without anchovies, the salad was not free of them: Worcestershire sauce contains anchovy. With Parmesan as well, it packs a lot of savoury depth for a bowl of lettuce.
The cookery writer Julia Child wrote that her parents took her to Cardini's restaurant as a child in the 1920s, and that she remembered the salad being tossed at the table.
The Caesar salad belongs with the fortune cookie as a food shaped by immigrants cooking for American customers. Cardini later bottled his dressing, and the brand still carries his name.
